top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on my common test. The random-coefficients demand framework changed what can be credibly known about substitution, market power and merger effects from market data. About three decades of use, critique and refinement in regulation and applied work have tested it. The credit core is a single jointly authored contribution, and the citation can be limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets without diffuse attribution. No prior-prize overlap is raised, though I have not verified this independently. The main caveats are that it is a methods prize and that estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form. A metascience view also holds that validation through use is not the same as systematic robustness testing. P002 (B030) is a strong design-based finding, but the persistence, magnitude and shift-share debates make it less mature, and it sits next to recent prizes. It still ranks above no award, because P000 would leave a well-supported contribution unrecognised.
